title: Lists can change
idea: Opener for the append/assignment unit: unlike a fixed number, a list can grow and its items can be swapped. Thinking first.

exercises.prompt: A shopping list in real life isn't fixed — you add things and cross things off. Which of these is 'adding to the list'?
exercises.explanation: Adding a new item makes the list longer. That 'grow the list' action is one of the two new powers in this unit.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is 'changing an item already on the list'?
options: Crossing out 'apples' and writing 'pears' in the same spot
Adding a brand-new line at the end
exercises.explanation: Replacing what's in a spot changes an existing item. That's the second new power: item assignment.

exercises.prompt: So far our lists have stayed the same size once written. This unit lets them grow.
exercises.explanation: Until now, a list was whatever you wrote. Now you'll add items to make it longer, and swap items in place.

exercises.prompt: Which real tasks involve GROWING a list (pick all)?
options: Recording each new score as players finish
Adding a guest to the invite list
Checking how many items there are
exercises.explanation: Recording each new score and adding a guest both make the list longer. Counting and reading don't change the list.

exercises.prompt: A list starts empty and you collect results one at a time. Why start empty?
options: You don't know the values yet — you'll add them as they arrive
You can never add to a non-empty list
exercises.explanation: Starting empty and adding as you go is a very common pattern — like a scoreboard that fills up during a game.

exercises.prompt: Match each action to what it does to a list.

pairs.left: Add a new item at the end
Replace the item at a spot

exercises.explanation: Adding grows the list; replacing keeps its size but swaps one value; counting leaves it untouched.

exercises.prompt: Replacing an item at a position does NOT change how many items the list has.
exercises.explanation: Swapping a value in an existing spot keeps the count the same — you changed WHAT is there, not HOW MANY.

exercises.prompt: A scoreboard shows [10, 20]. A new player scores 15. After adding, what should it show?
exercises.explanation: Adding puts the new score at the end: [10, 20, 15]. The list grew from two items to three.

exercises.prompt: A list shows [10, 20, 30]. You fix a typo: the middle value should be 25, not 20. After changing, what shows?
exercises.explanation: You replace the item at the middle spot: [10, 25, 30]. Same three items, one value corrected.

exercises.prompt: This unit teaches two new powers. What are they?
options: Adding an item, and changing an item at a position
exercises.explanation: Next you'll meet append (to add) and item assignment (to change a spot). Two tools for shaping a list.
